name: Aisha Ito

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I’m with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to employers, unions, AI firms or government. What you say is confidential. Tell me about a usual shift.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I’m Aisha Ito, 43, a junior worker on a commercial shop fit-out crew. I help fit counters and shelves, carry materials and ask the lead joiner to check my first cuts because I am still learning. I left school early, and I use an AI app every day to organise questions from the plan. The night premium puts my pay above the usual site rate, though I miss bedtime with the children.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What is the household depending on?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My partner works in childcare, and we have two school-age children and a mortgage. We have saved about nine months of expenses. I like that a good night shift turns an empty shop into a place people can use, but I would welcome more evenings at home if a daytime wage covered the loan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the night crew that my AI checklist saves me from forgetting a question, not from making a bad cut. On the bookshop fit-out, it reminded me to ask about the counter height before we fixed the supports. I still laid a tape across the floor myself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'm 43 and still learning general carpentry, which is easier to admit in a quiet shop than in front of a whole crew. The night premium lifts my pay and my partner's childcare wage is steady. With nine months of expenses saved, the mortgage and the children's school needs feel covered for now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep taking the fit-out shifts and have the lead joiner check the first counter support I install. In the first year I'd continue using AI each day to draft my task list, then cross out anything the drawing or site says is wrong. We would keep the monthly transfer into the mortgage overpayment account while night work stays available.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, and perhaps a little pleased. A modest tool that helps me remember a question is enough. I am not looking for a machine to make me an expert overnight.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What was wrong with the first counter plan?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The drawing used an old counter height, and the shop owner wanted a lower section for children. The app did not know that until I asked. I brought the question to the lead joiner before we fixed the supports, and we avoided cutting twice.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do nights cost you at home?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My partner handles most bedtime with our two school-age children. I see them at breakfast, then sleep before the next shift. The pay is good, but I would take a daytime rate if it covered the same loan payment.

say: I would say my daily **AI checklist** helps me remember questions before building.
I would tell coworkers the **tape** still settles the real measurement.
think: I am a **junior carpenter** who still needs a lead joiner’s check.
Our **nine-month savings** and two wages keep the mortgage secure now.
do: Keep paid **shop fit-out shifts** and request checks on first supports.
Draft a daily **AI task list** and correct it against the site drawing.
Continue monthly **mortgage overpayments** while night premiums last.
feel: **Calm** and pleased with a modest tool, without expecting instant expertise.
S0.quote: I am not looking for a machine to make me an expert overnight.
fieldNote: Aisha’s **counter-height question** shows she uses AI daily to prompt conversation, not replace real measurements.
Night work produces **higher pay** but costs family evenings, giving her a reason to value a viable daytime rate.

steps.text: Keep paid night fit-out shifts and request first-support checks
Use AI daily to draft task lists checked against the site drawing
Continue monthly mortgage overpayments while night premiums remain

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say booking, buying and customer replies could happen before we even unlock a shop, and that might shorten the fit-out. I would try a shared digital task board if it shows who changed a measurement. I would ask the manager to tell us whether faster jobs mean fewer night shifts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My hands still have work, but a short fit-out could use fewer junior workers if the plan arrives perfect. I do not think plans ever arrive perfect; I also cannot budget on being right about that. The night premium pays a useful piece of the mortgage, though our savings give us time if hours dip.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This week I'd offer to test the shared board on one aisle with the lead joiner, logging every change against the signed drawing. I'd use AI to list questions for the shop manager before each night shift. In the first year I'd keep paid shifts, then compare three months of payslips with the old pattern before asking nearby fit-out firms for openings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Excited by less confusion and nervous about shorter rosters. A board where I can see who changed the counter height would be a gift. A board that quietly makes my night shift disappear would be a different story.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make the board worth keeping?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We should be able to trace a changed shelf height to a person and a time, then check the signed drawing. Last month a verbal change traveled through three workers and came out wrong. I would keep the board if it cut that sort of rework.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you judge the pay effect?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would lay three payslips beside the last three from a similar job and look at total hours and premiums. My partner’s childcare wage is steady, but it is not enough to carry the whole mortgage comfortably. If the pattern turns down, I would apply while I still have work.

say: I would try a **shared task board** if changes can be traced to a person.
I would ask whether faster fit-outs mean **fewer night shifts**.
think: I might lose **junior hours** if better plans shorten jobs.
Our savings buy time, but the **night premium** supports the mortgage.
do: Test the **digital board** on one aisle with the lead joiner.
Use **AI questions** before shifts and check changes against signed drawings.
Compare **three months of payslips** before applying to nearby firms if pay falls.
feel: **Excited** by clearer revisions and nervous about the roster.
S1.quote: A board that quietly makes my night shift disappear would be a different story.
fieldNote: Aisha proposes a **one-aisle trial**, a bounded test grounded in a recent verbal change that went wrong.
She watches **total hours and premiums**, recognising that job retention may still mean lower mortgage income.

steps.text: Use AI and a shared board to check changes against signed drawings
Keep paid fit-out shifts while checking three months of payslips
Apply to nearby fit-out firms if total pay falls after three months

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell coworkers full thinking AI comes by 2028, and capable hands-on robots follow around 2031. The bookshop's planning and ordering may change first, but my joinery is on the later clock. I would ask to see a robot work in a cramped shop before trusting a showroom demonstration.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be 45 when thinking work changes and 48 when machines can do what my hands do. My daily AI use does not give me ownership of the future job. Nine months saved gives us a pause, not a new wage, and my partner's childcare pay cannot carry the loan alone for long.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep the night wage and ask the contractor for a paid trial of any site robot, with a safety supervisor present. This month I'd call the local trade college about a funded course in machine setup; I'd enrol only if there is practical work and employers name paid openings. In the first year after 2028 I'd apply for paid machine setup trainee posts, and postpone our planned family trip so the cash stays available.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I am worried and impatient to get real information. I would rather see one robot fail safely in a tight doorway than hear ten speeches about the future. A short runway makes waiting feel expensive.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why machine setup?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A cramped shop needs someone to decide where equipment can stand and what path stays open. I could learn that, but a fully capable robot might plan its own setup. I want a paid trainee post, not a slogan that operators will always be needed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell the children about the trip?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say we are putting it off for a year while we learn what happens to my work. We would still do local days out. I would not make the children responsible for a mortgage worry they cannot solve.

say: I would say **thinking AI** arrives by 2028 and capable site robots around 2031.
I would ask for a **cramped-shop trial** before trusting a robot demonstration.
think: I would be **48** when robots can do my hands-on joinery.
Daily AI use and **nine months saved** do not guarantee a new wage.
do: Keep the paid **night wage** while seeking a supervised robot trial.
Enrol in funded **machine setup training** if practical work and paid openings exist.
Apply for **trainee posts** after 2028 and postpone the family trip.
feel: **Worried** and impatient for real evidence within a short runway.
S2.quote: I want a paid trainee post, not a slogan that operators will always be needed.
fieldNote: She acknowledges **machine setup** may itself be automated, even while exploring it as a paid route.
The postponed **family trip** preserves existing cash; her children are spared responsibility for adult mortgage worries.

steps.text: Keep paid shop fit-out night shifts during the early AI change
Enrol in funded machine setup training if practical work and paid openings exist
Apply for paid machine setup trainee posts after 2028
Postpone the planned family trip for one year

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the crew the planning side changes by 2031 and site robots can match our physical work around 2034. Five years lets us test machines on awkward shops and write down failures. I would ask the contractor to include junior workers in trials, not only managers and salespeople.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At 48 I should have better joinery skills, and at 51 a robot could still do them. My children will be older, but the mortgage could still be there. I like having five years because I can find out whether machine setup work actually pays before committing our savings or dropping a night wage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep earning and build a record of two shop layouts where I spotted an access problem. I'd use AI each week to quiz me on plan symbols, with the lead joiner checking what I got wrong. If the trade college has a funded practical setup course with placements, I'd enrol; in the first year after 2031 I'd apply for setup or site maintenance openings only where employers are still hiring.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: More curious than afraid with this much warning. I would still feel the 2034 date when a machine came through the door. I can try something and change course if the first job route dries up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What access problem would you record?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At the bookshop, the planned shelving path blocked a fire exit while the counter was being fitted. We moved the materials and marked a clear route. I would photograph the corrected layout with permission because it shows a decision made in a real room.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you check placements?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would call two employers that hired the last course group and ask what those workers earn now. The college can tell me what it teaches, but the employers tell me whether a wage exists. I am willing to learn early, not to buy a badge for its own sake.

say: I would ask for **awkward-shop trials** and recorded failures before 2034 robots arrive.
I would include **junior workers** in those trials.
think: I would be **51** when capable robots reach my physical joinery work.
Five years allows me to verify **paid setup jobs** before risking savings.
do: Keep the **night wage** and document real access corrections.
Use **AI quizzes weekly** and check errors with the lead joiner.
Enrol in **funded practical training** with placements, then apply after 2031 where jobs remain.
feel: More **curious** than afraid, while aware the first job route may close.
S3.quote: I am willing to learn early, not to buy a badge for its own sake.
fieldNote: Her bookshop **fire-exit correction** supplies real evidence for a possible setup application.
She treats training as useful only when **employers confirm wages**, not because a course promises a future field.

steps.text: Keep paid night shifts and document permitted access corrections
Use AI weekly to quiz plan symbols and check errors with the lead joiner
Enrol in funded practical setup training if it has real placements
Apply for setup or maintenance openings after 2031 if employers hire

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell coworkers the office changes by 2036 and capable site robots arrive around 2039. A decade is long enough to measure real safety results and work out what training leads to wages. I would keep building now and ask for trials we can actually watch.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be 53 at the thinking change and 56 when robots can do my hands-on work. The children will be grown, so school pickups and school trips will not be the same burden. We may have paid much of the mortgage by then, but I cannot assume a pension or stop earning at 56.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing paid fit-outs while learning finish work and using AI for daily planning questions. My partner and I would put some night premium toward the mortgage twice a year after keeping our nine-month reserve. In the first year after 2036 I'd join a supervised robot trial and look for paid setup work if the contractor is actually employing people as 2039 approaches.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm about the near years. I would like to see fewer nights away from home before the children grow up. The longer clock gives us room to cut the loan and test a route without betting the house on it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you take a lower-paying daytime role?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If the mortgage balance is small enough and the daytime offer is real, yes. Being home at supper has a value I can name even if it is not on a payslip. I would compare the full household budget first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What must a trial show you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It must show who stops the robot, who checks a finished joint and what happens when the shop layout changes overnight. I would watch the machine in a real room, not only in a clear warehouse. A decade gives the contractor time to answer those questions.

say: I would ask for **real safety results** before 2039 site robots arrive.
I would tell the crew training matters only if it leads to **wages**.
think: I would be **56** when capable robots arrive, with grown children and perhaps a smaller loan.
I cannot assume **pension income** or a permanent setup job.
do: Keep paid **fit-out work** and use AI for daily planning questions.
Pay some **night premium** toward the mortgage twice yearly after protecting savings.
Join a **supervised robot trial** and seek paid setup work after 2036 if openings exist.
feel: **Calm** near term, with a wish for more evenings at home.
S4.quote: Being home at supper has a value I can name even if it is not on a payslip.
fieldNote: Aisha’s long-run goal is **fewer night shifts**, supported by debt reduction rather than assumed retirement.
She remains open to a **robot trial** only if it answers stop, inspection and changing-layout questions.

steps.text: Keep paid shop fit-outs and continue learning finish work
Use AI daily for planning questions checked against actual drawings
Pay some night premium toward the mortgage twice yearly after preserving savings
Seek paid setup openings after 2036 if the contractor still hires

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because site robots arrive around 2031, before I have much time to build a trade record. A paid practical course with actual jobs, a robot trial in a cramped shop and clear notice about night shifts would help. I would move quickly, but I need to see where a wage comes from.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn’t ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask how a new job fits family time. A role that keeps me employed but takes every evening from the children is not the same as a stable life. I would weigh the hours alongside the pay before changing crews.

headlineQuote: I would move quickly, but I need to see where a wage comes from.
portrait: Aisha is a **43-year-old junior** construction worker fitting shop counters and shelves after leaving school early.
Night premiums bring **higher pay**, and a childcare partner, nine months saved and a mortgage support two school-age children.
She uses **AI daily** to prepare questions, while checking real measurements with the lead joiner.
She tests **machine setup training** against paid openings and weighs future work against evenings with her family.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** leaves only until about 2031 before capable robots reach her hands-on fit-out work.
whatWouldHelp: A **paid practical course**, real job openings, cramped-shop trials and night-shift notice would support a decision.
